root.note: zayt, borrowed through Andalusian Arabic. The az- at the start of azeite reflects the Arabic article al- before z.

history: Portugal has two words for oil, and they come from two worlds. Óleo is Latin oleum, the oil in your car or the sunflower oil in a bottle. Azeite is olive oil, and it is Arabic: zayt with the article al-, which before z is pronounced az-. So the Portuguese word carries the Arabic ‘the’ inside it, like arroz and aldeia. The olive itself has the same pair. Azeitona, ‘olive’, comes from the Arabic word, while oliveira, ‘olive tree’, is Latin. At a Portuguese table azeite is everywhere: on bacalhau, on grilled fish, on bread. Spanish has aceite, from the same Arabic word, but in Spanish it means oil in general.
historyEinfach: Azeite means ‘olive oil’. The word comes from Arabic: az-zayt, ‘the oil’. Óleo is another word for oil; it comes from Latin. The olive is azeitona, from the same Arabic word. In Portugal people put azeite on fish, bacalhau and bread.

elsewhere.text: Arabic zayt and zaytūn, ‘olives’, are behind azeite and azeitona.
Same Arabic word, wider meaning: Spanish aceite is any oil, olive oil is aceite de oliva.
